article_title: Assessing the Influence of AI-Generated Responses on Academic Achievement: An Ethical Perspective and Self-Efficacy
citation: Oladayo, C. E., & Diri, E. A. (2026). Assessing the Influence of AI-Generated Responses on Academic Achievement: An Ethical Perspective and Self-Efficacy of Delta State Secondary School Students, Nigeria. Journal of Research in Mathematics, Science, and Technology Education, 3(4), 276–288. https://doi.org/10.70232/jrmste.v3i4.72
title: SQEIAIGRASQ questionnaire and Quadratic Equation Achievement Test (QEAT)
description: The study used two validated instruments: the "Students' Questionnaire on Ethical Impacts of AI-Generated Responses on Students' Achievement in Solving Quadratic Equations" (SQEIAIGRASQ), capturing students' ethical perspectives and self-efficacy, and the Quadratic Equation Achievement Test (QEAT) measuring achievement. Both were "validated by mathematics teachers and measurement and evaluation experts", and "Reliability testing showed a high reliability index".
requirements: Validation by mathematics teachers and measurement and evaluation experts, with corrections made
constraints: Designed for the quadratic-equations topic and Senior Secondary School I students in the Nigerian context
target_learning_goals: Measuring mathematics achievement in quadratic equations and students' ethical perspectives and self-efficacy regarding AI-generated responses
examples: Mean and standard deviation answered the research questions and independent-samples t-tests tested the null hypotheses using these instruments
key_sources: Oladayo, C. E., & Diri, E. A. (2026). Assessing the Influence of AI-Generated Responses on Academic Achievement: An Ethical Perspective and Self-Efficacy of Delta State Secondary School Students, Nigeria. Journal of Research in Mathematics, Science, and Technology Education, 3(4), 276–288. https://doi.org/10.70232/jrmste.v3i4.72

article_title: Training English language student teachers to become reflective teachers
citation: Ali Al-Issa & Ali Al-Bulushi. (2010). Training English Language Student Teachers to Become Reflective Teachers. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, Vol 35, 4. https://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajtec/vol35/iss4/4/
title: 25-item six-theme reflective-training questionnaire (Cronbach's Alpha = 0.868)
description: A five-point Likert questionnaire of 25 items was created to obtain student teachers' and trainers' attitudes about reflection approaches and strategies, validated by a panel of six specialist judges and piloted with ten randomly-selected student teachers, being "found to be highly reliable (Cronbach’s Alpha = 0.868)". Items were re-categorised under six themes: reflection through self-evaluation, formal instruction, observation, talking, practical experience, and research. It was administered on-line via Google Docs to 90 student teachers (a 39 per cent response rate) and to seven of eight e-mailed trainers (87.5 per cent).
requirements: Items achieving consensus among at least four judges were accepted
constraints: Only 90 of 230 final-year student teachers participated, a 39 per cent response rate
target_learning_goals: assessing approaches and strategies used to train student teachers to reflect on their teaching
examples: Administered on-line via free Google Docs forms at the end of the spring semester 2009, with responses automatically saved to Excel
key_sources: Ali Al-Issa & Ali Al-Bulushi. (2010). Training English Language Student Teachers to Become Reflective Teachers. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, Vol 35, 4. https://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajtec/vol35/iss4/4/

article_title: Implementing CBM: SQL-Tutor After Fifteen Years
citation: Mitrovic, A., & Ohlsson, S. (2015). Implementing CBM: SQL-Tutor After Fifteen Years. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0049-9
title: SQL-Tutor, the first constraint-based tutor for SQL querying
description: SQL-Tutor is an intelligent tutoring system for the SQL Select statement, designed as a complement to database courses that assumes students have some knowledge from lectures and labs. "The system provides numerous problem-solving opportunities in the context of various databases", which students can freely choose among. Its interface reduces working memory load by displaying the database schema and problem text, and it provides feedback at several levels of specificity, from simple correctness flags to hints and full solutions. The system has been in regular use in university database courses since the late 1990s.
requirements: Students should already have acquired some knowledge via lectures, labs and demonstrations
constraints: The system covers only the SQL Select statement, more precisely a subset of its language constructs
target_learners: university students learning SQL in database courses
examples: The 1998 evaluation used the Solaris version; a Windows version was downloaded 1946 times from May 1999 to January 2001, and a web-enabled version has been used since 1999
key_sources: Mitrovic, A., & Ohlsson, S. (2015). Implementing CBM: SQL-Tutor After Fifteen Years. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0049-9

article_title: A Framework System for Intelligent Support in Open Distributed Learning Environments—a Look Back from 16 Years Later
citation: H. Ulrich Hoppe. (2015). A Framework System for Intelligent Support in Open Distributed Learning Environments—a Look Back from 16 Years Later. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 504–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0058-8
title: SQLSpaces tuple-space middleware for loosely coupled learning environment components
description: SQLSpaces is the COLLIDE group's own implementation of the Tuple Space concept, replacing the IBM T-Spaces implementation to achieve loose coupling of agents that communicate indirectly through notes in a shared-memory space. Generic clients were provided for languages including Java, JavaScript, Prolog, Python and C#. Giemza et al. (2007) showed how a classical AIED error-diagnosis approach could be re-implemented on this basis with little extra effort, and SQLSpaces was used in the SCY project for collaborative inquiry learning.
requirements: A blackboard/tuple-space architecture so agents communicate indirectly through notes in the space rather than direct agent-agent communication
target_learners: learners in distributed collaborative learning environments, e.g. science inquiry projects
examples: Weinbrenner et al. (2010) used this multi-agent architecture based on SQLSpaces for monitoring and detecting (un-)systematic behavior of learners working with a simulation tool
key_sources: H. Ulrich Hoppe. (2015). A Framework System for Intelligent Support in Open Distributed Learning Environments—a Look Back from 16 Years Later. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 504–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0058-8

article_title: A Framework System for Intelligent Support in Open Distributed Learning Environments—a Look Back from 16 Years Later
citation: H. Ulrich Hoppe. (2015). A Framework System for Intelligent Support in Open Distributed Learning Environments—a Look Back from 16 Years Later. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 504–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0058-8
title: Learning analytics gadget framework based on SQLSpaces and Activity Streams
description: In the Go-Lab project the authors abandoned the Kaleidoscope common logging format in favor of Activity Streams, and Manske et al. (2014) describe a flexible framework for authoring reusable and portable learning analytics gadgets based on SQLSpaces and Activity Streams. A general analysis workflow is applied to learner-generated concept maps to form an aggregate or overlay map, which is presented to learners as a metacognitive scaffold in a web-based learning space to support group reflection.
requirements: Action logging in a portable format (Activity Streams) and the SQLSpaces middleware
target_learners: learners working collaboratively in web-based learning spaces
target_learning_goals: group reflection supported by metacognitive scaffolds
examples: Figure 2 illustrates the processing chain from analysis workflow to overlay concept map to embedded learning analytics gadget
key_sources: H. Ulrich Hoppe. (2015). A Framework System for Intelligent Support in Open Distributed Learning Environments—a Look Back from 16 Years Later. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 504–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0058-8

article_title: Preparing preservice teachers to teach with digital technologies: An update of effective SQD-strategies
citation: Jo Tondeur, Ottavia Trevisan, Sarah K. Howard, Johan van Braak. (2025). Preparing preservice teachers to teach with digital technologies: An update of effective SQD-strategies. Computers & Education 232. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105262
title: SQD2: an updated Synthesis of Qualitative Data model of strategies for preparing preservice teachers to teach with digital technologies
description: SQD2 is a revised evidence-based model structuring strategies for developing preservice teachers' digital competencies across micro, meso and macro levels, updating the original 2012 SQD model. It consolidates 28 sub-categories into 10 categories and six synthesised statements, including familiarisation, reflective practice, collaborative design, a cycle of authentic experiences and feedback, an affective dimension, and institutional vision. The authors report that "new categories and most importantly new relationships among them emerged through the current study", with exploration foregrounded and the meso level reframed around pedagogy, commitment and the affective dimension.
requirements: Strategies must address both micro-level preparation of preservice teachers and meso-level institutional conditions, with attention to relationships among categories rather than treating them separately
constraints: Derived from a meta-aggregation of 28 qualitative studies published between 2012 and 2024, so the model reflects qualitative evidence from that window only
target_learners: preservice teachers in teacher training institutions
target_learning_goals: digital competence for integrating digital technologies in teaching and learning
examples: The review aggregated 28 sub-categories into 10 categories and six synthesised statements, presented in Figs. 3–8 and consolidated into the SQD2 model in Fig. 9
key_sources: Jo Tondeur, Ottavia Trevisan, Sarah K. Howard, Johan van Braak. (2025). Preparing preservice teachers to teach with digital technologies: An update of effective SQD-strategies. Computers & Education 232. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105262

article_title: The Effect of Teaching Strategies and Curiosity on Students' Achievement in Reading Comprehension
citation: Busmin Gurning & Aguslani Siregar. (2017). The Effect of Teaching Strategies and Curiosity on Students’ Achievement in Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 10(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n11p191
title: SQ3R reading comprehension strategy
description: SQRRR or "SQ3R" is a reading comprehension strategy named for its five steps: survey, question, read, recite, and review, introduced by Francis Pleasant Robinson. It offers a more efficient and active approach to reading textbook material and helps students build a framework to understand their reading assignment. In this study it served as the control (comparison) teaching strategy.
requirements: Must be used with a text that is unfamiliar to the students, though students should have some background knowledge
The teacher prepares ahead of time by reading the book and deciding in advance where the stopping points will be for each section
target_learners: Senior high school (grade XI) EFL students; originally created for college students
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension of textbook and exposition texts
examples: In the study, the control class of 38 students was taught with SQ3R over the same six meetings; low-curiosity students in this class outperformed low-curiosity INSERT students.
key_sources: Busmin Gurning & Aguslani Siregar. (2017). The Effect of Teaching Strategies and Curiosity on Students’ Achievement in Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 10(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n11p191

article_title: Effect of the SQ4R Technique on the Reading Comprehension of Elementary School 4th Grade Elementary School Students
citation: Başar, M. & Gürbüz, M. (2017). Effect of the SQ4R Technique on the Reading Comprehension of Elementary School 4th Grade Elementary School Students. International Journal of Instruction, 10(2), 131-144. http://www.e-iji.net/dosyalar/iji_2017_2_9.pdf
title: SQ4R technique (Survey, Question, Read, Reflect, Recite, Review)
description: SQ4R is a whole-process reading strategy the article describes as "especially designed for the use in explanatory and descriptive texts", developed from SQ3R after Applegate et al. (1994) added the Reflect step. It comprises six steps: Survey (skimming headings, illustrations and bold words), Question (preparing questions from sub-headings), Read, Reflect (answering and summarising without the textbook), Recite, and Review. In the study it was taught to fourth-graders over ten weeks, first modelled by the researcher, then implemented independently by students.
requirements: questions should definitely be prepared and should ensure that students are focused on the meaning of the text
constraints: the article describes it as designed for explanatory and descriptive texts
examples: The experimental group received Turkish language classes using SQ4R for ten weeks, one hour per week, with the researcher modelling the technique in the first two weeks.
key_sources: Başar, M. & Gürbüz, M. (2017). Effect of the SQ4R Technique on the Reading Comprehension of Elementary School 4th Grade Elementary School Students. International Journal of Instruction, 10(2), 131-144. http://www.e-iji.net/dosyalar/iji_2017_2_9.pdf

article_title: The Effect of Using the "SQP2RS via WTL" Strategy through Science Context to 10th Graders' Reading Comprehension in English in Palestine
citation: Ziad Mohammed Mahmoud Qabaja, Jamal Subhi Ismail Nafi’, Maisa’ Issa Khalil Abu-Nimah. (2016). The Effect of Using the “SQP2RS via WTL” Strategy through Science Context to 10th Graders’ Reading Comprehension in English in Palestine. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.26. https://www.iiste.org
title: SQP2RS six-step reading strategy framework integrated with Writing to Learn
description: The SQP2RS strategy, introduced by Vogt (2002) within the SIOP model, is a multi-step instructional framework for teaching reading whose steps are surveying, questioning, predicting, reading, responding and summarizing. The article describes how each step works — for example, in the survey step “the teacher leads students through whatever text is to be read by modeling their own thinking process,” and in the summarize step students work in pairs or groups to summarize the text’s key concepts using key vocabulary. The researchers integrated Writing to Learn (WTL) into all steps so students take notes, answer questions and write summaries, and prepared a teacher’s guide of activities applying the combined strategy to the tenth-grade English curriculum in Palestine.
requirements: Teacher modeling of each step the first time it is used, which Ruddel (2008) indicates is important for later effective use
A teacher’s guide with reading texts, objectives, pictures, a worksheet, a poster and activities implementing the strategy
constraints: The study applied the strategy through science context with 10th graders in Bethlehem district public schools in the first semester of 2015-2016
target_learners: 10th grade EFL students in public secondary schools
target_learning_goals: English reading comprehension of content-area texts
examples: The experimental group was taught five units, each consisting of three reading periods, using the strategy over three months
key_sources: Ziad Mohammed Mahmoud Qabaja, Jamal Subhi Ismail Nafi’, Maisa’ Issa Khalil Abu-Nimah. (2016). The Effect of Using the “SQP2RS via WTL” Strategy through Science Context to 10th Graders’ Reading Comprehension in English in Palestine. article_title: Improving 4th Grade Primary School Students' Reading Comprehension Skills
citation: Aydın Bulut. (2017). Improving 4th Grade Primary School Students' Reading Comprehension Skills. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(1): 23-30. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.050103
title: SQ3R (Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review) as a five-stage reading comprehension strategy
description: SQ3R is a reading comprehension strategy with five stages: Survey, Question, Read, Recite and Review. In the Survey stage readers skim "the main titles, subtitles and abstract and visuals"; in the Question stage titles are transformed into questions; Reading is an "active" attempt to answer those questions; Recite has students answer questions in their own words; and Review revisits notes and re-reads if necessary. The article describes it as one of the oldest and most common reading strategies, developed to provide a more productive reading process that improves comprehension, memorization and time management.
requirements: Implementation across all five stages, with data collection tools designed to be suitable for all stages of the strategy as in this study
constraints: The article reports students may experience difficulties at some stages, particularly Recite
target_learners: primary school 4th grade students with reading comprehension difficulties
examples: Eight texts suitable for the students' level were adapted for SQ3R and implemented 3 hours a day, 3 days a week for 10 weeks with seven 4th graders
key_sources: Aydın Bulut. (2017). Improving 4th Grade Primary School Students' Reading Comprehension Skills. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(1): 23-30. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.050103
